deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivations. It is a set of verbatim excerpts, in Riemann's hand, from G. Lamé, 'Leçons sur la théorie mathématique de l'élasticité des corps solides' (Paris 1852). The heading reads 'Excerpte aus Lamé. Leçons sur la théorie mathématique de l'élasticité des corps solides.' There are three excerpts.

(1) p. 11 (Leçon II). Lamé compares two definitions of the elastic force (stress).
- The first definition is molecular: the elastic force on a surface element is the resultant of the molecular actions between the molecules on either side of it, across a thin zone.
- The second is the 'quicker' definition: stress as a force applied to a surface.
- He argues that 'force applied to the surface' is a vague expression. The pressure of a gas on a solid must be understood as repulsive actions from several solid layers on several gas layers. This raises doubts about whether gas density near the wall equals the density far away.
- Traction and the sense of touch likewise involve actions between layers at a distance.
- Hence the first definition is the only complete one. He nevertheless adopts the second, supported by the analogy with tensions.

(2) pp. 35–37 (Leçon III, §14, 'Extension aux solides cristallisés'). Lamé's methodological claim: his new mode of demonstration leaves undetermined the mutual influence of different kinds of matter, with no hypothetical attraction or repulsion laws. If the problems can be put into equations this way, the forces and their laws will follow as consequences. This mirrors theoretical astronomy, where universal attraction was not the starting point but a forced consequence of the laws of motion (Kepler to Newton).

(3) pp. 37–38 (§15, 'Méthode par l'intégration autour d'un point'). Lamé criticises Navier and others for deriving the elasticity equations by integrating molecular forces around a point, which presupposes continuous matter. Poisson merely replaced one integral sign by an unevaluated Σ while performing the other two integrations. The sentence ends at 'dont on trouve l'origine dans les travaux' and continues on the page given as 'previous' ('de M. Cauchy ...'). So this folio actually precedes that page in reading order.

Implicit technical content (my addition, not on the page): the Navier–Poisson molecular method gives the one-constant theory λ = μ, hence Poisson ratio 1/4. The Cauchy/Green/Lamé approach keeps λ and μ independent. Riemann's selection shows his interest, for his Naturphilosophie, in the methodological question: deduce force laws from phenomena rather than assume action-at-a-distance laws.
errors: No mathematical errors; this is a copied text. Possible copying slip: 'dans la zone voisine du fluide' is semantically odd and probably should be 'voisine du solide' (the zone of the gas adjacent to the solid). The manuscript appears to read 'du fluide', so this may be Riemann's or Lamé's wording; check against Lamé 1852, p. 11.

results.what: Stress (elastic force) defined as the resultant of molecular actions across a surface element vs. as a surface-applied force
results.modern_name: Cauchy stress concept / molecular interpretation of stress

results.what: Methodological program: derive force laws as consequences of the field equations, analogous to Newton deducing gravitation from the laws of motion
Critique of Navier–Poisson 'integration around a point' (it assumes continuity of matter and leads to λ=μ)
results.modern_name: Rari-constant vs multi-constant controversy in elasticity

deep.surprise_reason: These are reading excerpts copied from Lamé's well-known 1852 textbook. There is no original mathematics, and Riemann's interest in Lamé and molecular physics for his Naturphilosophie is known.

checkable.asserts: The Navier–Poisson one-constant theory (λ=μ), criticised in the excerpt, gives Poisson ratio 1/4.
With λ=μ, Young's modulus E = μ(3λ+2μ)/(λ+μ) equals 5μ/2, a rari-constant 'formule usuelle' contradicted by experiment.

transcription_corrections: The ending 'dont on trouve l'origine dans les travaux' continues on the page labelled 'previous' ('de M. Cauchy ...'), so this folio precedes it in reading order.
'III. §. 14.' is written as an interlinear insertion above '(„Extension aux solides cristallisés")', between 'p. 35 & 36.' and the title; the opening quotation mark before Extension is present.
'dans la zone voisine du fluide': the manuscript seems to read 'du fluide', but Lamé's sense suggests 'du solide'; check against the printed source.
